Sign errors are caught by scripts/verify-data.ts, which scores the calibration fixtures in data/config/calibration.json. Reverse-scored items (q3, q7, q17, q19, q27, q29, q30) are deliberately interleaved to catch acquiescence bias — do not cluster them. q29 and q30 were added after measurement showed that skipping Q23 alone changed the top-ranked policy lever, because restraint_capacity and inside_outside each rested on a single item while carrying the highest policy weight (1.3) and being the only policy axes every lever has a value on. sections.title: The misalignment chain
sections.blurb: Three separate links. People who agree on the first often split on the third, and that split routes to entirely different work.

sections.title: Where leverage lies
sections.blurb: What is actually binding, and who is best placed to relieve it.

questions.text: How likely is it that AI systems capable of fully automating AI research arrive before 2032?
If such systems arrive, how likely is a software-only intelligence explosion — large capability gains without a corresponding hardware buildout?
Scaling and algorithmic progress will hit hard limits that push transformative capability past 2040.
Systems trained with roughly current methods end up pursuing goals meaningfully different from what their developers intended.
Current models already show real misalignment rather than ordinary capability failure.
Given misaligned goals, how likely is it that systems will conceal them and behave well under training and evaluation?
Misaligned systems will mostly fail visibly rather than strategically.
Given a scheming system deployed at scale, a well-resourced developer could still catch and contain it before catastrophe.
Safety measures that assume the model is adversarial can work without solving alignment.
Allocate 100 points between two sources of harm.

allocation_poles.low: People using AI systems for exactly what they intended
allocation_poles.high: AI systems doing what nobody intended

questions.text: Seizure of durable power by a small group is a likelier catastrophe path than loss of control.
Competition between states is the primary driver of unsafe development.
Biological or cyber misuse by non-state actors is a top-three risk.
If AI goes badly, it's more because we didn't know how to build it safely than because we knew and did it anyway.
A talented safety researcher does more good inside a frontier lab than outside one.
Labs' published safety commitments meaningfully constrain their behavior.
Working at a lab mainly confers legitimacy on the lab.
Safety requires understanding internal computation, not only testing behavior.
Behavioral evaluation can in principle provide sufficient assurance.
Effort belongs on making current architectures safe rather than designing new ones.
Formal guarantees are worth pursuing at large cost to practicality.
How likely is it that AI systems will do a large share of alignment research themselves before it matters?
Policy should constrain what companies can do rather than build state evaluation capacity.
Holding a government position beats influencing from outside.
The most valuable thing government can add is the independent ability to evaluate frontier systems — not new restrictions on what companies may build.
Would you take a role that publicly and durably associates you with one political party?
The AI policy ideas that ended up mattering were developed outside government and carried in, rather than originated by people holding office.
Would you work in an administration whose stated AI priorities differ substantially from yours?
Avoiding catastrophe is nearly sufficient — a good long-run outcome follows fairly naturally from there.
Whether AI systems are moral patients should shape how the field allocates effort now.
